articles.title: Donald Trump to meet NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani at Gracie Mansion during UNGA visit
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump is set to meet New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday at Gracie Mansion, the mayor's official residence, as Trump trav.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump is set to meet New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday at Gracie Mansion, the mayor's official residence, as Trump travels to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.The meeting will focus on issues affecting New York City and its residents, Mamdani's communications director Anna Bahr said. The White House confirmed the meeting but did not provide further details, as reported by AP.The meeting comes despite the often-contentious political relationship between Trump and Mamdani. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, defeated former Governor Andrew Cuomo in the Democratic primary before winning the mayoral election in November. He has frequently been targeted by Republicans.Trump, however, has struck a notably warmer tone toward Mamdani since the mayor's election. During their first meeting after Mamdani won, Trump described the encounter as cordial and said the then-mayor-elect would “surprise some conservative people.” That marked a contrast with Trump's description of Mamdani during the 2025 campaign as a “100% Communist Lunatic.”The two have also previously used their meetings to discuss federal support for New York. During a February meeting, Mamdani handed Trump a mock New York Daily News front page reading “Trump to City: Let's Build.”The headline was a play on the newspaper's famous 1975 front page, “FORD TO CITY: DROP DEAD,” which referred to President Gerald Ford's pledge to veto federal financial assistance to New York.Mamdani's aides said the mock front page was intended to highlight the potential public reaction to new federal investment in housing and the support such funding could receive in the city.Trump's meeting with Mamdani comes as New York hosts nearly 130 world leaders for this year's UN General Assembly, with wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as concerns over artificial intelligence, among the major issues confronting the gathering.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Offer ‘tips’ to good officers, says Karnataka minister, lands in soup
articles.summary: Hassan minister KM Shivalingegowda faces backlash over “tips” remark to officials at Prajaseva meet; BJP slams comment, minister says statement was misread.
articles.body: HASSAN: Hassan district minister KM Shivalingegowda’s statement that there is “nothing wrong” if citizens happily give ‘tips’ or ‘honorarium’ to govt officials for timely work has triggered outrage among the public and BJP.The minister made the comment during ‘Prajaseva Andolana’, a public-grievances meet, here Saturday.Puneeth, a farmer from Alur taluk in the district who was attending the meeting to highlight his land case, condemned the statement in front of the minister. “Officials are paid a salary. Why should we give them tips? Doesn’t this amount to encouraging bribery?” Puneeth and a group of youths questioned the minister directly. With more people backing them, the meeting witnessed chaos.Sensing the situation going out of hand, Shivalingegowda tried to defend himself. “I meant officials should not extort money. I said honest workers should be respected, not that bribery should be encouraged,” he said.The minister Sunday clarified: “A person complained that bribe was being sought to get his work done. I told him not to give any money, but to respect the officer. My statement has been misunderstood,” Gowda said.Deputy commissioner KS Latha Kumari pacified the protesters. “The minister’s statement has been misinterpreted. If officials demand bribes for work, stringent legal action will be taken against them,” she said.BJP MLC CT Ravi, on his ‘X’ account, condemned the minister for his remarks. Ravi has mentioned that chief minister D K Shivakumar had said that if anyone asks for even Rs 10 as a bribe, complain to him. articles.title: 93% of deleted Bengal voters have won appeals, EC tells SC
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Around 93% of those whose cases have been decided so far over not being able to vote in the West Bengal polls this year because of doubts r.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Around 93% of those whose cases have been decided so far over not being able to vote in the West Bengal polls this year because of doubts raised about their eligibility during Election Commission's SIR drive have won their appeals and have been included in the electoral roll. However, 8,649 of 1.2 lakh lost their appeal and will be deleted.The numbers, mentioned in an annexure to an affidavit filed by EC in Supreme Court, showed that 1,13,943 could satisfy the tribunals that the commission's decision to exclude them from the roll was incorrect, and this may intensify criticism of the poll panel.Curiously, while the affidavit - filed to counter the claim of TMC and its MP, Derek O'Brien, that the exclusions cost them 31 assembly seats - puts the number of cases decided until Sept 16 at 1,26,194, the annexure stated that 1,22,592 were decided by the 24 tribunals until Sept 10.EC sources, however, said the number of disposed of cases was too low to be seen as representative of the final outcome of all cases. They also said the results might favour inclusion because cases where citizens had documentary proof were decided first.The annexure also mentioned district-wise filing of appeals by voters and disposal of cases. The appellate tribunals were set up on SC's direction that panels comprising former HC chief justices and judges would hear appeals against exclusions in the roll revision process. A person whose claim for inclusion was rejected could approach the tribunals, which had started hearing appeals in April.Claiming that O'Brien had misled the court, EC said, "It is pertinent to note that the applicant has conspicuously ignored the other side of the very same data relied upon by it. As disclosed in the applicant's own application, in as many as 21 constituencies, the number of deletions under adjudication exceeds the margin of victory of the candidates belonging to the applicant's own party."The affidavit said that applying the very same test and reasoning propounded by the applicant, "the applicant would, therefore, equally have to seek setting aside of the election results in those constituencies won by its own party candidates"."The selective and inconsistent application of an inherently flawed and speculative yardstick, therefore, exposes the self-serving and mala fide nature of the present application," it said.EC said the attempt to portray all deletions as "effective disenfranchisement" was wholly incorrect and misleading. "It is humbly submitted that even assuming, without admitting, the correctness of the figures relied upon by the applicant, once the removals pertaining to ineligible ASDD (absent, shifted, duplicate/dead, and demoted/displaced) entries are excluded, the applicant's own data demonstrates that in several constituencies, the number of adjud-icated deletions is lower than the margin of defeat," it said.This data, therefore, "completely demolished" the "speculative theory that the adjudication exercise altered the electoral outcome," the affidavit said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Xi prepares China ‘for battle’ as expert warns of grave danger facing US ahead of DC summit
articles.summary: China expert Gordon Chang claims Xi Jinping is preparing China for war against the U.S. as President Donald Trump hosts a high-stakes summit Thursday.
articles.body: As President Donald Trump touts a productive relationship with China ahead of his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, an expert is warning that the U.S. is in a "very dangerous period" in its relations with the communist nation, claiming that Xi is preparing for war. Trump and Xi are set to meet on Thursday in Washington, D.C., just four months after the leader’s last meeting in May, with artificial intelligence and trade expected to be at the forefront of the conversation. Gatestone Institute senior fellow Gordon Chang claimed that, despite the leaders trumpeting a positive relationship, Xi is mulling a war against the United States and organizing troops "for battle." TRUMP SAYS CHINESE PRESIDENT XI JINPING WILL VISIT US ON SEPT 24 "Xi Jinping keeps on talking about going to war against us… and also he's preparing China's society, civilian and military, for battle. And we think we're at peace," Chang said Sunday on "Fox News Live." "So, this is a very dangerous period for us." Chang’s remarks come amid reports that China aided Iran in attacks that killed three U.S. troops in Jordan earlier this summer. TRUMP SAYS CHINA 'SPIES' ON US AFTER REPORT TIES CHINESE IMAGERY TO IRAN STRIKE Iran reportedly received satellite images of an airbase in Jordan from Chinese entities before carrying out the attack, according to the Wall Street Journal. Chang decried China for providing "targeting data" to Iran that resulted in the deaths of U.S. service members, saying Trump must "absolutely" get tougher on China and arguing that decades of open dialogue with the Chinese have only made things worse for the United States. EXPERT WARNS CHINA ALREADY WAGING ‘UNRESTRICTED WARFARE’ AGAINST US THROUGH FENTANYL, ESPIONAGE AND SABOTAGE "Whatever one thinks of the strategic discussions the United States has with China, there's this moral dimension that China is deliberately killing Americans," he said. Experts expect this week’s summit with Trump and Xi to be vastly different from their May meeting, as since then, conflict in the Middle East has escalated and the AI race has intensified. articles.title: California tightens disclosure rules for influencers who post political ads
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill imposing criminal and civil penalties on content creators who fail to disclose paid political advertisements, a measure aimed at bringing greater transparency to the growing use of influencer marketing in politics.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill imposing criminal and civil penalties on content creators who fail to disclose paid political advertisements, a measure aimed at bringing greater transparency to the growing use of influencer marketing in politics. The bill, AB1130, was signed into law Saturday as part of a series of new measures that Newsom’s office said are aimed to “protect elections in California from interference and political meddling.” Though existing laws required someone to disclose whether they were being paid to post, there was no liability provision that officials could use to enforce the rule. Now, authorities will be allowed to impose penalties under the Political Reform Act of 1974 that can include a misdemeanor charge, according to the law’s text. Influencers are playing a growing role in political campaigns, as candidates and political groups seek to reach people who increasingly turn to social media for news and information. Some creators are paid by campaigns or outside groups to produce political content, while others post about candidates and issues without compensation. Assembly member Marc Berman, who proposed the legislation, said the growing influencer industry has “changed the way candidates communicate with voters.” “As more candidates pay influencers to post content supporting their campaigns, it is imperative that voters have the right to know whether or not that content is organic and authentic or paid political messaging,” Berman said in a statement last month, as the bill was headed to the governor’s desk. The issue came to the forefront earlier this year during billionaire climate activist Tom Steyer’s more than $200 million campaign for California governor, which he lost. Steyer’s campaign paid social media influencers to post favorable content about him, but many of the posts did not disclose that the creators had been paid, according to a May report by the Los Angeles Times. The undisclosed posts prompted a complaint to California’s Fair Political Practices Commission alleging that the campaign had violated the state’s disclosure requirements for paid political content. A campaign spokesperson told the Los Angeles Times that all the rules were followed in hiring content creators, describing the complaint as “baseless.” The case involving the complaint remains open, according to the commission’s website. Researchers at the Information Integrity Institute at the University of Tennessee’s College of Communication and Information published a report last month in which they examined what transparency measures social media users in the U.S. want from paid political influencers. Their study, in which they surveyed about 1,000 U.S. social media users through the platform Prolific, found that “participants who placed a greater value on authenticity were also more likely to support disclosure when political content was paid for.” “One of the more real problems is not just you see something that’s completely false or you see something that’s completely true, but you see inauthentic or misleading propagandist-type opinions pushing people’s perspectives in different directions,” associate professor Benjamin Horne said in a blog post about the findings. The institute’s director, Catherine Luther, added that she believes “any movement towards transparency in online information is a good thing. I think it can only be beneficial for democratic societies.”

articles.title: Tensions escalate in Middle East ahead of high-stakes UN General Assembly. Here’s what to know
articles.summary: As world leaders prepare to gather in New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) this week, a growing number of flashpoints across the Middle East are raising concerns about a wider regional escalation, from renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen to fresh warnings exchanged between Washington and Tehran.
articles.body: As world leaders prepare to gather in New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) this week, a growing number of flashpoints across the Middle East are raising concerns about a wider regional escalation, from renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen to fresh warnings exchanged between Washington and Tehran. Why are the Houthis and Saudi Arabia back at the center of regional tensions? A dramatic Houthi offensive in Yemen has emerged as one of the most significant developments heading into UNGA. The Iran-backed group has seized key territory in recent weeks, including a strategically important island in the Red Sea and coastal areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a crucial maritime chokepoint linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. US and Gulf officials have expressed growing concern that the Houthis are seeking to establish greater control over the waterway, which is vital to global trade and energy shipments. Despite receiving increased US intelligence and targeting support, Saudi Arabia has struggled to halt the Houthi advance. CNN reported Friday that Gulf and American officials are increasingly doubtful Riyadh can reverse the Houthi gains on its own. The fighting has intensified sharply in recent days. Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, Islam’s holiest city, while the Houthis claimed they shot down a Saudi F‑15 fighter jet over Yemen. On Saturday, the group also claimed missile and drone attacks on “sensitive” sites in Riyadh and an Aramco oil facility in Yanbu. The latest exchanges underscore fears that Yemen is becoming an increasingly important front in the broader regional confrontation involving Iran. Why are US embassies warning Americans? Amid the worsening security environment, the US State Department and several US diplomatic missions have urged Americans in the region to exercise increased caution. On Saturday, the State Department warned that the conflict “has the potential to escalate rapidly” and advised heightened vigilance. Separately, the US Embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a security alert restricting travel by US government personnel to the cities of Taif and Yanbu without special authorization. The warnings come as officials monitor the possibility of additional attacks involving Iran, Iranian-aligned groups and US partners in the region. What are Iran and Trump saying? Iran’s central military command said Sunday it had received information suggesting the United States, with support from regional partners, could be preparing new military action against Iran. In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim News Agency, Iran warned that any new US attack would trigger sustained strikes on US bases and interests across the region. Tehran also warned that countries assisting such operations would be considered parties to the conflict. There have been no publicly reported US strikes on Iran for more than two weeks. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, further raised tensions with remarks indicating major decisions on Iran may be approaching. Speaking to Fox News, Trump said he was in “deciding mode” and that “very big things” could happen soon. According to Fox correspondent Trey Yingst, Trump outlined three possible outcomes for Iran: a deal with Washington, increased economic pressure or military action. At the same time, Trump said his administration remains in contact with the Houthis and is still avoiding direct US military involvement in the group’s conflict with Saudi Arabia. Which Middle East leaders will be at UNGA? Regional diplomacy is expected to be dominated by discussions on Iran, Yemen, maritime security and energy markets. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan is leading a delegation, while Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain are all sending senior representatives. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also expected to attend the General Assembly after the Trump administration approved travel for a core Iranian delegation. “Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week,” a State Department spokesperson said Thursday. With fighting intensifying in Yemen, threats escalating between Washington and Tehran, and energy markets remaining sensitive to disruptions, many diplomats arriving in New York see this year’s General Assembly as taking place under one of the most volatile Middle East security environments in recent years.

articles.title: Qatar PM describes fallout of US-Israel war on Iran as ‘earthquake’
articles.summary: Speaking before the UN General Assembly, Sheikh Mohammed also announces a key shift in Qatar’s investment strategy.
articles.body:
Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani has called on states to respect sovereignty as a condition for security in the Middle East, warning against “cycles of escalation” after “an earthquake” caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.

The region needs a “framework in which sovereignty is respected” and no state can pose a “threat to another”, Sheikh Mohammed said on Sunday at the opening of the Qatar Economic Forum’s UN General Assembly-adjacent event in New York City.

Sheikh Mohammed – who is also Qatar’s foreign minister – described the economic fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran as “an earthquake” with “its shock waves” reaching far beyond the borders of the Middle East, “challenging assumptions about security and stability”.

“During the crisis, almost every conversation began with security and de-escalation, then turn[ed] to energy supplies, shipping routes, and with our investments, plans will continue. These were different expressions of the same question. When so much is being disrupted, what can still be relied upon?”

He said that Qatar has weathered the test to the “foundations” of the country’s economy and security, but acknowledged that the ongoing conflict in the region is having an impact.

“Permanent security cannot be built through arrangements that leave any state permanently exposed to insecurity,” Sheikh Mohammed said. “We must address the sources of tensions and build confidence.”

Reporting from New York, Al Jazeera’s Kristen Saloomey said that message “no doubt will be repeated” when Gulf leaders meet US President Donald Trump on Tuesday during the UN General Assembly.

The PM also outlined a domestic shift in Qatar’s investment strategy by pledging more than $38bn in spending on Qatari infrastructure over the next five years.

“That’s meant to attract private investors and send a message of Qatar’s resilience,” Saloomey said, while the PM is nonetheless acknowledging that the ongoing conflict is “having an impact on the region”.

The UNGA starts on Monday and ends on Friday.

The situation in the Middle East and its global ramifications are expected to be high on the agenda during speeches and diplomacy.

Also on Sunday, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed Al-Ansari, told US media in New York that the mediation efforts by his government are ongoing to restart talks between Tehran and Washington to end the US-Israel war on Iran.

articles.title: US prepares sweeping sanctions on International Criminal Court
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration is preparing sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court that could restrict most of the Hague-based tribunal.
articles.body: The Trump administration is preparing sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court that could restrict most of the Hague-based tribunal's financial transactions and potentially cut it off from much of the global banking system, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing US officials and documents.The measures would take effect after a six- to seven-month grace period and could prevent the court from conducting transactions in US dollars, according to the report. Transactions involving communications services would be exempt.Meanwhile, a State Department spokesperson pointed to Ssecretary of stateMarco Rubio's view that the ICC threatens US sovereignty.The administration could finalise the measures as early as this week, during the UN General Assembly in New York, or in the days that follow, according to the Journal.The proposed sanctions would go beyond existing US measures, which have targeted individual ICC officials including former chief prosecutor Karim Khan, ICC President Tomoko Akane, judges, deputy prosecutors and the prosecutor who led the case against Israeli officials.Washington's confrontation with the court intensified after the ICC issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity linked to the Gaza war. Both have rejected the allegations.Rubio said in July that the administration would pursue a broad campaign against the court and would dismantle it "brick by brick" if necessary. He has argued that the ICC overstepped its authority by pursuing officials from countries that are not members of the court, including the United States and Israel.The US and Israel are not members of the ICC.The administration's position has drawn attention to Rubio's earlier stance on the court. As a US senator in 2022, he co-sponsored a resolution supporting an ICC investigation into alleged war crimes in Ukraine committed by Russia, another non-member state. The ICC later issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin.European countries and other major ICC supporters, including Japan, have pledged to defend the court against US pressure, although it remains unclear what measures they could take to shield its operations from the proposed sanctions.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Eighteen suspects extradited to US over Haitian president’s 2021 killing
articles.summary: Federal court in Florida to try men accused of orchestrating the transnational plot to kill Jovenel Moise from US soil.
articles.body:
Eighteen suspects facing federal charges for the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise have been flown to the United States.

A military flight on Sunday transported the suspects from the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, to the US state of Florida, where the defendants are set to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the transnational plot to kill the former leader.

The major development comes after federal prosecutors in the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida successfully secured convictions in May against what they called “gang leaders” and “co-conspirators” implicated in the scheme to kill Moise.

The high-profile investigation is being directed by US Attorney Jason A Reding Quinones, an appointee of US President Donald Trump.

“Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination of President Jovenel Moise,” Quinones wrote on social media. “We will follow the evidence wherever it leads, to those who financed it, facilitated it, supported it or committed crimes to make it possible. Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished.”

Quinones did not immediately identify the suspects being extradited, but those who remain in Haiti awaiting trial include more than a dozen Colombian soldiers and a former Haitian government official.

Quinones said that the FBI and others “remain steadfast in ensuring that all individuals who allegedly sought profit from the assassination of a head of state are held fully accountable”, with FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles confirming that multiple arrests in the US and abroad were made on Sunday.

Moise, 53, had been shot dead overnight at his private residence in the Pelerin 5 neighbourhood, in the hills above Port-au-Prince in July 2021, while his wife was critically injured. His killing caused a profound political vacuum that left the Caribbean nation devoid of any elected national leader. Capitalising on this institutional collapse, armed gangs have rapidly expanded their influence, ultimately consolidating control over an estimated 90 percent of Port-au-Prince.

At least 8,100 gang killings were documented in 2025, with insecurity displacing about 1.5 million people, according to the United Nations.

Legal jurisdiction was established by US federal courts in Florida, the closest US state to Haiti, because the overarching plot to assassinate Moise had been primarily engineered, financed, and staged out of the southern part of the state, according to federal prosecutors.

A fair trial inside Haiti had also grown increasingly impossible owing to the ongoing security collapse and entrenched graft stemming from intense gang violence, political chaos and overlapping humanitarian crises that have severely paralysed and hollowed out the judicial system.

In Haiti, prominent human rights activist and executive director of the National Human Rights Defense ⁠Network Pierre Esperance said that the transfer ⁠of the 18 suspects to the US was a “disgrace for the Haitian justice system”, and called for an overhaul of the judicial system to allow such complicated cases to be tried inside Haiti in the future.

In May, a jury in Florida convicted four men in the killing, and at least five others have pleaded guilty and are serving life sentences.

No national elections have been held in Haiti since Moise’s assassination.

articles.title: Zelensky to meet with Trump in New York this week
articles.summary: President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky are meeting in New York City this week, the Ukrainian leader said Sunday. “I just spoke with President Trump @POTUS. An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelensky…
articles.body:
President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky are meeting in New York City this week, the Ukrainian leader said Sunday.

“I just spoke with President Trump @POTUS. An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelensky wrote on social media Sunday.

Trump is set to give an address to the United Nations General Assembly meeting on Tuesday . He is also meeting with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) on Monday.

“I thanked the President for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s visit to Kyiv,” Zelensky said in his post, referencing a recent Ukraine trip by U.S. envoys Witkoff and Kushner.

“We went through the key details thoroughly, and they saw the situation in Ukraine firsthand. The peace track is our number one priority,” he added. “There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life.”

Earlier this month, Witkoff said the U.S. was confident that trilateral talks would lead to a “good resolution” to the war in Ukraine following his and Kushner’s meeting with officials in Kyiv.

The war in Ukraine will hit the five-year mark in February, and the Trump administration has made a concerted push throughout the president’s second term to end the conflict, one of the major issues central to U.S. foreign policy at the moment.

articles.title: AI fears burst onto Trump-Xi agenda, but challenges abound
articles.summary: Apocalyptic warnings about the danger of uncontrolled artificial intelligence are adding new urgency to talks between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping set for next week. Trump has dismissed AI’s existential threats as a “hoax” — a view that analysts say aligns with China’s general perspective. Intense competition for primacy and mutual distrust have…
articles.body:
Apocalyptic warnings about the danger of uncontrolled artificial intelligence are adding new urgency to talks between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping set for next week.

Trump has dismissed AI’s existential threats as a “hoax” — a view that analysts say aligns with China’s general perspective. Intense competition for primacy and mutual distrust have so far delayed any conversations between the U.S. and China about AI safeguards and regulations.

But recent warnings from the U.S. tech industry and calls to slow down innovation have put the need for American-Sino cooperation higher on the agenda between Trump and Xi when the two meet in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24.

Trump on Friday told reporters AI would be among many things being discussed next week. And Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Axios on Wednesday he’s open to talks about “shared risks” around AI in talks with Beijing.

There are also high-profile champions of AI caution in China — although for different reasons.

China’s top spy chief warned in an article published last week that AI could pose a direct threat to the Chinese Communist Party’s hold on power, an unusually blunt and public call to arms in a tightly controlled political and media environment.

“We’re at a point where both the United States and China appear to agree on some of the risks posed by AI, particularly around issues of cyber capabilities and loss of control,” said Alison Szalwinski, senior vice president at strategic and capital advisory firm The Asia Group.

“The challenge is that there’s some really significant disagreements on how to manage those risks, and whether AI governance can be separated from the broader strategic U.S.-China competition.”

Expectations are low for Trump and Xi to announce any breakthroughs on the top issues of the bilateral relationship: trade, Taiwan and technology transfers. Their hotly anticipated summit in Beijing in May was largely viewed as heavy on ceremony and light on substance.

There’s even lower odds for a major breakthrough on AI security or safeguards this time around. The most that analysts are looking forward to is whether Washington and Beijing can set up a format for dialogue about AI.

“At this point, the immediate goal is less about negotiating a major AI agreement, we’re just not there yet, and more about establishing a durable channel for discussing frontier AI risk,” Szalwinski said.

One of the main concerns for the U.S. is AI development inside frontier labs, which pose the greatest risk of AI breaking out from under human control and carrying out catastrophic actions related to weapons deployment and infrastructure shutdowns, among other potential threats.

In a Sept. 8 social media post, one artificial intelligence researcher warned that AI developers believe the technology could kill off humanity by the end of the decade. A few days later, Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, called for the heads of these major companies to commit to slowing down development to allow safety regulations to keep up.

But Amodei also warned that the U.S. must maintain an advantage over China’s AI development, calling it a national security imperative and lashing out at Chinese companies’ “distillation” — using American AI models to speed up developing their own technology.

Beijing took exception to being labeled a threat.

“Fear-mongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only hamper efforts toward sound global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” Guo Jiakun, spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry, said in response to questions about Amodei’s manifesto.

Guo added that “All parties should jointly promote the open and inclusive development of AI for good and for all.”

That position is likely more in line with Trump, said Kyle Chan, a fellow in the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution.

“I don’t think that Trump is feeling any pressure about the existential AI risk issue. He calls it a hoax multiple times. It reminds me very much of how he treats climate change,” Chan said.

“I think his primary concern is keeping the AI boom going, keeping the stock market going, keeping the data center boom going.”

But Bessent’s caution on AI and influence within the administration is likely to move forward talks with China. An important question is who Xi will assign as Bessent’s counterpart and what that will signal.

Candidates include Ding Xuexiang, China’s tech industrial czar; the heads of China’s National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), who largely responsible for managing China’s domestic economy; or top officials with China’s Cyberspace Administration (CAIC).

“Depending on which of those two would send a different signal,” Chan said, referring to the latter two options.

“The NDRC head has been involved in investment talks and joint AI development talks with other countries … CAIC would be a signal about a more serious discussion about AI regulation and safety.”

Establishing AI talks between the U.S. and China is one challenge but then agreeing on what to discuss is another major hurdle.

In 2024, former President Biden and Xi agreed that humans — not AI — should control nuclear arms, and Democratic lawmakers included that directive in federal law, a provision in the 2025 National Defense Authorization Act.

Democrats want Trump to bring that up with Xi when they meet next week.

And Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), the ranking member of the House Select Committee on China, is convening a virtual hearing the day before Xi’s visit to raise discussions around how to pace AI development responsibly and address shared risks, featuring experts in the field.

“We urgently need an agreement with China on basic inspections and safety standards,” Khanna said in a statement.

He struck out against what he said was silence from leading American artificial intelligence companies to testify at the hearing.

“After multiple requests to OpenAI and Anthropic, they haven’t committed to testifying,” he added, raising the possibility of subpoenas if Democrats take the majority after the midterms.

Republicans are largely deferring to Trump’s position of not wanting to do anything that will hamper America’s competitive edge.

Still, some are hawkish on making sure Trump holds Xi’s feet to the fire in protecting against Chinese theft of American technology and restricting U.S. commercial sales that could give Chinese companies an edge.

The U.S. should “slow down” China’s AI development “as much as possible” by limiting access to advanced AI products, Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), the chair of the House Select Committee on China, wrote to Trump in a letter on Friday .

“I encourage you to ensure that no one in your administration is granting the PRC [People’s Republic of China] any concession or pause in policy action that could contribute to the PRC’s attempts to catch up to the U.S. and overtake our lead in AI,” he wrote.

articles.title: McDonald’s once sold beloved cookies featuring forgotten characters from the chain's past
articles.summary: McDonald's discontinued McDonaldland Cookies featured Grimace and Ronald McDonald faces with a subtle lemon flavor that fans still crave decades later.
articles.body: Introduced in 1974, McDonaldland Cookies became a regular addition to McDonald’s Happy Meals when they debuted nationwide in 1979, but the beloved menu item was discontinued in the early 2000s, to the disappointment of many fans. The small, crunchy, cookies were baked for McDonald’s by Keebler, had a subtle lemon flavor and featured the faces of beloved McDonald’s characters like Grimace, Ronald McDonald, Birdie, and Hamburglar. Customers described them as a cross between shortbread and animal crackers, and McDonaldland Cookies came in either a little plastic bag or a brightly colored cardboard box that also showed the faces of McDonald’s characters. The fast food chain altered its Happy Meals to include healthier items such as apple slices in the early 2000s. MCDONALD'S REVIVES DECADES-OLD FAVORITE FOR AMERICA 250 AFTER YEARS OF CUSTOMER REQUESTS Between 2003 and 2004, McDonaldland Cookies were discontinued at all U.S. locations. Chocolate chip cookies, however, remained on the menu. McDonald’s has been serving some variation of chocolate chip cookies since the early 1970s, with today's chewy, soft-baked version introduced in 2012. MCDONALD'S BRINGS BACK POPULAR ITEM FOR SHORT TIME AS ONE STATE GETS A TREAT Although McDonaldland Cookies are no longer available in the United States, select McDonald’s locations in Australia still offer them, and certain New Zealand restaurants serve the treat under the name "McHappy Cookies." Fans have also shared on Reddit that a cookie with a flavor and texture similar to the original McDonaldland cookies is available at Aldi supermarkets. AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS One Reddit user commented: "I am eating the Benton's animal crackers from Aldi right now and they taste exactly like the McDonaldland cookies." McDonaldland Cookies might be gone in the U.S., but the characters have not been totally forgotten. The viral Grimace Shake, a purple-hued milkshake with a vanilla soft serve base and mixed berry flavoring, came out in 2023 as a limited-time treat to celebrate the beloved character’s birthday. Beginning in 2022, McDonald's sporadically released various limited-edition Adult Happy Meals, allowing grownups to enjoy the nostalgia of Happy Meals — which, depending on their age, might have included McDonaldland Cookies. articles.title: Bill Goldberg bought a California estate for $1 million in 1999; he expanded it to 28 acres with a 20-car “Garage Mahal”
articles.summary: News News: WWE Hall of Famer and former NFL player Bill Goldberg listed his Eagle Mountain Estate in Bonsall, California, for $3.2 million in November 2019, afte.
articles.body: WWE Hall of Famer and former NFL player Bill Goldberg listed his Eagle Mountain Estate in Bonsall, California, for $3.2 million in November 2019, after spending two decades expanding the property around the home he bought in 1999. Goldberg paid about $1 million for the original estate, which covered roughly 17.5 acres at the time, and subsequently acquired neighbouring parcels that brought the total holding to 28 acres. The property combined a 4,630-square-foot house with equestrian facilities, riding trails, a pool and a custom-built 6,800-square-foot garage designed to accommodate Goldberg's collection of vintage vehicles. The garage, known as the "Garage Mahal", had been featured on television programmes including Garage Mahal and Dream Garages. By the time the property went on the market, Goldberg and his wife, Wanda, had already moved to Texas and taken his car collection with them.Goldberg bought the original property in 1999The house was built in 1997, two years before Goldberg purchased it. Realtor.com reported that Goldberg paid $1 million for the property in 1999, when the estate covered approximately 17.5 acres. Over the following years, he bought three neighbouring parcels as they became available, expanding the combined property to 28 acres. The resulting Eagle Mountain Estate was situated on a secluded section of Bonsall, north of San Diego. The property was entered through a gated private driveway surrounded by mature landscaping, with a small creek and a koi pond near the entrance. Hunter & Maddox described the estate as being designed to appeal to automobile enthusiasts, equestrians and prospective vineyard owners. The estate was listed for $3.2 million in November 2019. Listing agent Richard Combs of Hunter & Maddox told Realtor.com that the property was particularly likely to attract car collectors because of the scale and design of Goldberg's garage.The house covered 4,630 square feetThe single-level main residence measured 4,630 square feet and contained four bedrooms and four bathrooms. The interior included a large kitchen and family room, living room, office and dining room with vaulted ceilings. The property also featured custom stonework and a private entrance surrounded by landscaping. Outside, the estate included a swimming pool and spa with a waterfall and slide, a half basketball court, fire pit and sitting area. A separate guesthouse was also part of the property. These features sat alongside the estate's more unusual automotive and equestrian facilities. The acreage also gave the property a potential agricultural use. Hunter & Maddox noted the possibility of establishing a vineyard, while the property's existing landscape included citrus and avocado orchards. The listing described the surrounding vegetation as habitat for butterflies, bees and hummingbirds.The 6,800-square-foot garage was bigger than the houseThe most distinctive part of Eagle Mountain Estate was its custom-built garage. At 6,800 square feet, it was roughly 2,170 square feet larger than the main residence and had space for at least 20 vehicles. Goldberg designed and oversaw the garage to house his collection, and it became known as the "Garage Mahal". The structure was more than a basic storage facility. Reporting on the listing described car lifts, car-washing areas, display lighting, custom flooring and storage for spare parts. It also included a gym and additional living space, making it closer to a private enthusiast's facility than a conventional residential garage. The garage had also appeared on television, including Goldberg's Garage Mahal and Dream Garages. Despite its prominence in the sale, however, Goldberg's actual collection was not included with the property. Realtor.com reported that he had already taken the cars with him after moving to Texas with his wife.The estate also had horses, riding trails and vineyard potentialFor buyers more interested in horses than cars, the property included a four-stall horse facility and more than 15 miles of riding trails. Hunter & Maddox said the trails passed through areas surrounded by citrus and avocado orchards. The combination of acreage, climate and existing landscaping also gave the property potential for vineyard development. articles.title: England and Wales to have specialist courts for rape cases
articles.summary: Victims will have a private entrance and a private waiting room to separate them from defendants.
articles.body:
Specialist courts to handle cases of rape and other sexual offences will be introduced across England and Wales over the next two years, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced.

Each crown court will have at least one courtroom especially set up to hear such cases.

They will offer victims private entrances and waiting rooms to separate them from defendants, and there will be new training for court staff and fixed dates for trials.

Rape Crisis England and Wales welcomed the measures, which are expected to cost around £23m, as a "significant step forward" for the justice system that addressed a number of reforms it had been requesting for many years.

"Taken together, they reflect the urgency of ensuring that courts are fit for purpose and properly meet the needs of victims and survivors, which is crucial to securing justice," said the charity's chief executive, Ciara Bergman.

The government said the changes follow Labour MP Charlotte Nichols showing "immense strength and bravery" in speaking publicly about being raped and calling for changes to the justice system.

Nichols waived her automatic right to anonymity in March when she made a Commons speech and described having to wait more than 1,000 days to go to court.

Under the new measures, to be funded out of the Ministry of Justice budget, court staff will be given "trauma-informed training" and a single person of contact will be assigned to each survivor.

From next month, trials will be given a fixed date rather than placed on floating lists in what Burnham said was an effort to "rebalance the scales of justice and put victims first".

Earlier this year, the government announced that rape victims would be given access to specialist legal advice throughout the criminal justice process.

MP reveals rape ordeal during court reform debate

Delays to my rapist's trial left me terrified, survivor tells BBC

Rape victims to get specialised legal advice in courts

'Rape victims failed by court delays' say charity

Woman dropped sex assault case after court delays

Labour promised in its 2024 manifesto to halve violence against women and girls within a decade.

"For too long, victims of rape and serious sexual offences have felt let down by our justice system," Burnham said.

"Prosecution rates for rape remain shamefully low, with many victims waiting years for justice. This is not good enough."

The changes were "long overdue" and would make a "significant difference" but focusing on prosecution alone would not be enough, he added.

"So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place," the prime minister said.

Nichols spoke publicly for the first time about being raped when she accused the then Justice Secretary, David Lammy, of using crime victims as a "cudgel" to push through his reforms of the legal system.

She was criticising the Courts and Tribunals Bill's plans to limit jury trials to cases with a likely prison sentence of three years or more.

She said she had waited 1,088 days to go to court, with every day being "agony" and the "trauma" made worse by her role in public life.

Her attacker, she said, was acquitted at crown court but subsequently ordered to pay compensation after she won a civil case against him.

"It is because I have been raped that I am as passionate as I am about what it means for a justice system to be truly victim-focused," she said.

"It is because I have endured every indignity that our broken criminal justice system could mete out that I care what kind of reform will actually deliver justice for survivors and victims of crime more widely."

Responding to news of the specialist courts being rolled out, the Conservatives said tackling delays to criminal rape trials was "long overdue" and they pushed Labour to commit to scrapping plans to restrict jury trials.

"The fact that victims have been withdrawing their cases because they have taken too long has been a disgrace," said shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy.

"Labour need to get courts sitting throughout the year, end the delays and clear the backlog – not undermine our right to a trial by jury."

Last year another charity, the Salford Survivor Project, said victims of rape and sexual assault were being "failed by the system" as court backlogs reached a record high.

The long delays for cases to go to trial were having a serious impact on victims' mental health, it said.

Also last year, a woman who says she was sexually assaulted by a taxi driver on her 21st birthday told BBC News she had dropped the case because of court delays.

She reported the alleged incident in early 2022 and gave evidence in court in December 2023 but the case was adjourned until September 2024 when the judge fell ill.

"I made the decision, even though I hate the statement, to drop the case," she said. "I couldn't let this hurt me further."

The Crown Prosecution Service said that, without her testimony, the case had been dropped because of insufficient evidence.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

articles.title: ICE officer shoots man in Austin, Texas, officials say
articles.summary: An ICE officer shot and wounded a person Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas, officials said.
articles.body: An ICE officer shot and wounded a person Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas, officials said. The victim, who was identified as a man, was transported to a local hospital and is “in serious but stable condition” after being shot in the torso, Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said at a news conference. Austin Mayor Kirk Watson said the Austin Police Department was not involved in the incident. It was not immediately clear what the victim’s nationality is and whether he was a target of an ICE operation. Those questions “still need to be answered,” Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said. The shooting occurred around 1 p.m. in North Austin. Davis said a “small foot pursuit” occurred. Austin police investigators are on the scene and she is in contact with Homeland Security Investigations and other state law enforcement agencies, she added. “A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry,” Watson said at the news conference. “While I’m unhappy and I’m angry about it, I’m not surprised at all.” U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, said he is demanding an independent investigation, the release of body camera footage and “accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law.” “Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened. We can see the lies with our own eyes. We will demand truth, transparency and accountability,” he said in a post on X. Watson said he has asked for the city of Austin to be involved in any forthcoming investigations so that the police department can “be in a position to offer clear third-party eyes and expertise” Protesters gathered at the site of the incident following the shooting. One woman, who said she has lived in Austin for 33 years, told NBC News that she has never witnessed an incident like this and it “broke my heart.” NBC News has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and the White House for comment. In July, an ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national, in Houston during an attempted traffic stop to conduct an immigration arrest.

articles.title: Mike Vrabel snaps at reporter over Drake Maye's struggles after Pats win: 'you're not going to ruin my Sunday'
articles.summary: Mike Vrabel told reporters they wouldn't ruin his Sunday after the Patriots beat the Steelers 20-3, but Drake Maye's struggles still loom large.
articles.body: The New England Patriots got their first win of the season Sunday, and head coach Mike Vrabel wasn't about to let a few perfectly valid questions about his quarterback spoil the celebration. After New England defeated the Pittsburgh Steelers 20-3, Vrabel had a tense exchange with Boston Globe reporter Ben Volin, who pressed him about his level of concern over Drake Maye's performance through the first two weeks of the season. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Vrabel wasn't interested in entertaining the question. "You're not going to ruin my Sunday," the coach fired back. The exchange continued when reporter Greg Bedard also questioned Vrabel about Maye's struggles, prompting the coach to make it clear that he wasn't going to dwell on the negatives after a victory. To be fair, though, the reporters had a legitimate reason to ask. Maye hasn't exactly looked like the quarterback who led New England to the Super Bowl last season, and Sunday's win over Pittsburgh did little to put those concerns to rest. The 23-year-old completed 14 of 22 passes for 208 yards, no touchdowns and one interception against the Steelers. While he connected with receiver Romeo Doubs for a 63-yard gain, the Patriots struggled to consistently move the ball and finished with just 13 offensive points. Instead, New England's defense did most of the heavy lifting, holding Aaron Rodgers and the Steelers to just 3 points and 235 total yards. Rookie running back TreVeyon Henderson provided the Patriots' only offensive touchdown with a 39-yard run in the first quarter. Later, Christian Barmore strip-sacked Rodgers, and Elijah Ponder returned the fumble 19 yards for a touchdown to put the game away. In other words, the Patriots won comfortably, but Maye wasn't exactly the reason why. Sunday's performance came just 11 days after a disastrous season opener against the Seattle Seahawks. In a rematch of Super Bowl LX, Maye threw three fourth-quarter interceptions as New England blew a 10-point lead and lost 13-10. His final interception came in the end zone with just 26 seconds remaining, ending a potential game-tying drive. Maye finished that game with 178 passing yards, one touchdown and three interceptions. Afterward, he acknowledged that he had abandoned the patient approach that had worked earlier in the game. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "We had the game under control," Maye said following the loss. "Thought we had a good plan to start chipping away and be patient and lost patience, and it cost us, decisions that cost us the game on my part, on my end." Through two games, Maye has thrown four interceptions and just one touchdown pass. That's a far cry from his 2025 campaign, when he threw for 4,394 yards and 31 touchdowns while finishing as the runner-up in NFL MVP voting. No need to overreact. But with New England's franchise quarterback — so far — struggling to recapture last year's form, the questions about his performance aren't going away simply because Vrabel wants them to.

articles.title: France to summon Iran envoy after language centre closure in Tehran
articles.summary: Iran accuses the French language centre of conducting ‘illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions’.
articles.body:
France will summon Iran’s ambassador and take “appropriate measures” after Iranian authorities closed a French-language centre linked to its embassy in Tehran, according to the French Foreign Ministry.

“This new attack against France’s cultural presence in Iran , following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and unacceptable,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement on Sunday.

Iran announced on Sunday the closure of the centre it accused of conducting “illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions”.

“Based on the Tehran prosecutor’s office, the illegal centre affiliated with the French embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, was closed,” the Iranian judiciary’s Mizan news website said, referring to the French Language Centre (CLF).

It said the centre “abused its status as a language training facility” and sought to “identify and build networks among the country’s elite figures while facilitating their departure”.

The French Foreign Ministry said it would “take appropriate measures to respond” and would summon Iran’s ambassador in Paris at the request of French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot.

Relations between Tehran and Paris have been strained in recent months.

In August, Iran’s Intelligence Ministry said it detained two French diplomats over alleged foreign interference during a national security investigation before handing them over to the French ambassador.
